description: Parallel execution rules. onestop decomposes work into a task DAG, groups tasks into waves that can safely run at the same time, and fans them out to independent agents. The binding constraint is never the dependency graph - it is the WRITE SURFACE. Two agents editing the same file concurrently corrupt it, and no amount of speed is worth that.

algorithm: 1. READY = every task whose dependencies are all complete.
2. Order READY by longest remaining path through the DAG - the critical path goes first, because the wave is only as fast as its slowest lane.
3. Walk the ordered list and add a task to the wave only if its write surface is DISJOINT from every task already in the wave.
4. Cap the wave at max_width. A task that collides, or overflows the cap, waits for the next wave.
5. Dispatch the whole wave in ONE message - several Agent calls in a single assistant turn is what makes them concurrent. Dispatching them in separate turns is sequential execution wearing a costume.
6. Join: collect every result before scheduling the next wave.
7. Verify at the join, not inside the lanes - run the suite once for the wave.
8. Repeat until the DAG is drained.
scheduling.max_width_note: Five concurrent lanes is the practical ceiling. Beyond that the join summary stops being readable, token cost rises faster than wall-clock falls, and a failure in one lane becomes hard to attribute.

write_surface.rule: Every task declares the files and directories it will WRITE, before the wave is formed. Two tasks may share a read surface freely; they may never share a write surface inside one wave.
write_surface.declaration: Paths come from the plan `touches` field, which discovery populated. A task that cannot declare its write surface is not ready to be parallelised - run it alone.
collision_examples: Two tasks both editing src/routes/index.ts - collide, even if they add different routes.
Two tasks both adding a migration - collide; migration ordering is global state.
Two tasks both editing the same test file - collide.
One task writing src/api/orders.ts and another writing src/ui/OrderList.tsx - disjoint, safe.

A task writing a shared barrel/index/registration file that several features must touch - this is the most common hidden collision. Detect it and serialise those tasks, or have ONE task own the barrel and the others declare no write to it.
write_surface.shared_file_strategy: When several tasks must all register into one file (a route table, a DI container, an export barrel, a translations file), do not parallelise around it. Either give one task ownership of that file for the whole wave, or add a final serial task that performs every registration at once.

in_process.when: Write surfaces are disjoint - the normal case.
in_process.how: Plain parallel Agent calls in one message. No isolation needed; the partition already guarantees safety.

worktree.when: Two large lanes genuinely need the same files, or a lane is experimental and may be discarded.
worktree.how: Pass isolation: worktree on the Agent call. Each agent gets its own git worktree, so even overlapping writes cannot collide.
worktree.cost: A checkout per lane, and a real merge afterwards. Worth it for substantial independent lanes; overkill for a two-file change.
worktree.merge: Merge worktrees one at a time, running the suite after each. Never merge them all and then test - you lose the ability to attribute a failure.

always_parallel.note: These are read-only or write-disjoint by construction. Running them sequentially is the largest avoidable waste in the pipeline, and there is never a reason to.
cases: Discovery scouts - one per flow step, always independent.
Reviewers - code, security, data, accessibility all read the same diff and write nothing.
Per-component test runs where the components are independent.
Web and app automation - different targets, different files.

never_parallel.note: Speed is never worth these. Each is serialised regardless of what the DAG says.
cases: Database migrations - ordering is global and a concurrent apply corrupts state.
Any two tasks writing the same file, for any reason.
Dependency manifest edits - two agents writing package.json or the lockfile will clobber each other.
Git operations - commit, rebase, branch, push. One writer only.
The final registration/barrel task, if one exists.
Anything destructive or externally visible - a deploy, a data backfill, an outbound send.
Tasks whose acceptance criterion depends on another task in the same wave having finished.

failure_policy.rule: A failed lane never silently poisons the wave. Lanes are independent by construction, so the others are allowed to finish - stopping them wastes work already paid for.
steps: Let every other lane in the wave run to completion.
At the join, report exactly which lane failed and why, with its output.
Do NOT schedule any task that depends on the failed one.
Schedule the next wave from the tasks that are still unblocked - progress continues around the failure.
Retry a lane at most once, and only for a transient cause (a flaky network, a lock). Never retry a logic failure; fix it.
If the failure invalidates the plan, stop scheduling and return to the user with what completed and what is now uncertain.
failure_policy.never: Never report a wave as successful when a lane failed. Never merge a worktree whose lane failed.

speculative.note: Work that can start before it is strictly unblocked, because it only needs a completed subset.
cases: Review a finished slice while later slices are still being implemented. Findings arrive earlier and the review phase shrinks to whatever remains.
Generate automation for flow steps already implemented while the rest are in progress.
Write documentation for a stabilised contract while implementation continues against it.
speculative.guard: Speculative results must be re-validated at the real join. A review of code that later changed is stale - re-review only the delta, not the whole file.

reporting.requirement: Every wave reports a lane table. A bare speed claim is not a report, and an unexplained wave is impossible to debug.
reporting.shape:
WAVE <n>  (<k> lanes)
  lane | task | agent | write surface | result | duration
  join: <suite result>  |  next wave unblocked: <task ids>  |  blocked: <task ids and why>
